qs.q: A 54-year-old man presents with acute oliguria and rapid laboratory deterioration over two days. Investigations reveal a serum urea of 28 mmol/L and serum creatinine of 420 umol/L, yielding a urea-to-creatinine ratio of 22:1. What is the most likely cause of his acute kidney injury?
o: Renal artery obstruction from a tumour
qs.e: A urea-to-creatinine ratio greater than 20:1 strongly points toward a pre-renal cause of AKI due to reduced renal perfusion. Intrinsic conditions like acute tubular necrosis typically display a lower ratio because tubular damage impairs urea reabsorption.

ai.title: Serum Urea in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Serum urea reflects renal filtration and nitrogen balance. In low‑resource settings it helps detect acute and chronic kidney injury, guide fluid management, and flag uremic complications.

sections.p: Serum urea is the amount of nitrogen in the blood derived from protein catabolism, normally 7–20 mg/dL. It is measured by the urea–cyanate method and reported as BUN.
b: High BUN suggests impaired renal clearance or increased protein catabolism

t.b: Elevated BUN indicates reduced glomerular filtration or increased production; normal BUN with high creatinine suggests non‑renal causes.

sections.p: BUN is used with creatinine to stage acute kidney injury (AKI) via KDIGO criteria: Stage 1 (BUN 1.5–2× baseline), Stage 2 (2–3×), Stage 3 (>3× or >4 mg/dL).

t.b: Use BUN/creatinine ratio and absolute BUN to classify severity.

sections.p: In East Africa, the leading causes of raised BUN are dehydration, diarrhoea, malaria, HIV‑associated nephropathy, and herbal nephrotoxins. Other common contributors include urinary tract obstruction, sepsis, and rhabdomyolysis.

t.b: Proteinuria suggests glomerular disease; haematuria points to obstruction or infection.
Red cell casts = glomerulonephritis; granular casts = tubular injury.

sections.p: Patients with high BUN may be asymptomatic or present with fatigue, anorexia, nausea, oliguria, or altered mental status if uremia develops. In acute settings, dehydration may cause hypotension and tachycardia.

t.b: Confusion, lethargy, or seizures suggest severe uremia.

sections.p: Beyond BUN, a full renal panel is essential. In resource‑poor settings, a simple urine dipstick and bedside creatinine measurement can guide urgency.

t.b: Granular casts = tubular injury; red cell casts = glomerulonephritis.

sections.p: Severe hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, pericarditis, and cerebral oedema are life‑threatening complications of high BUN and require immediate action.

t.b: Peaked T waves, widened QRS, sine waves.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first: re‑hydrate, stop nephrotoxins, manage infections. Supportive care includes fluid balance, electrolyte correction, and monitoring for uremic symptoms.
b: Dialysis if uremic pericarditis, refractory hyperkalaemia, or severe acidosis

t.b: Uremic pericarditis, refractory hyperkalaemia, or severe acidosis.

sections.p: Repeat BUN/creatinine every 24–48 h in AKI, monitor urine output, and counsel on avoiding nephrotoxins. Vaccinate against hepatitis B and treat HIV promptly.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >6.5 mmol/L), oliguria/anuria, altered mental status, pericardial rub, or refractory acidosis

faq.q: Why is BUN higher than creatinine in dehydration?
faq.a: Volume depletion reduces glomerular filtration, concentrating urea more than creatinine, raising the BUN/creatinine ratio.
Yes, severe malaria causes rhabdomyolysis and sepsis, both of which impair renal perfusion and increase BUN.

faq.q: What is the safest way to re‑hydrate a patient with high BUN?
faq.a: Start with isotonic saline, monitor urine output and electrolytes, and avoid over‑correction to prevent fluid overload.

exam: A 35‑year‑old man with HIV presents with oliguria and BUN 60 mg/dL, creatinine 3.5 mg/dL. What is the next step? — Assess volume status, start isotonic fluids, and check for obstruction.
A patient with BUN 45 mg/dL and K⁺ 6.8 mmol/L develops a peaked T‑wave ECG. What is the priority treatment? — Immediate calcium gluconate and insulin‑glucose.
A 50‑year‑old woman has BUN 18 mg/dL but creatinine 2.5 mg/dL. What does this suggest? — Reduced GFR with normal BUN, likely chronic kidney disease.
Why is the BUN/creatinine ratio useful in differentiating prerenal from intrinsic AKI? — A ratio >20 suggests prerenal azotemia; a ratio <15 points to intrinsic injury.
What is the main limitation of using BUN alone to diagnose AKI in low‑resource settings? — It cannot stage AKI without creatinine and may be influenced by protein intake or dehydration.
A child with severe diarrhoea has BUN 25 mg/dL and creatinine 0.5 mg/dL. What is the likely cause of the elevated BUN? — Volume depletion leading to prerenal azotemia.
